title: Maintaining Long-Lived jQuery Applications
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of maintaining long-lived jquery applications in a jQuery application.
Apply auditing dependencies in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify documenting legacy behavior with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: This lesson covers maintaining long-lived jquery applications from a maintenance perspective. Examples prioritize current jQuery 4 behavior; older patterns are shown only to recognize and replace them.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns auditing dependencies into a repeatable implementation choice. Compatibility work begins with the official upgrade guide, a dependency inventory, tests, and a controlled migration plan. Do not teach removed APIs as current jQuery 4 functionality.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local HTML page with jQuery 4.0.0 loaded before app.js for JavaScript snippets. HTML and package-manager snippets can be checked as configuration examples. Run the interaction in browser DevTools, inspect the DOM/Network panel, and compare actual behavior with the expected result. Do not submit learner code to the production API for arbitrary execution.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original markup and code, clear console/network filters, reload the local page, and repeat the same interaction. For a request example, return the mock endpoint to its original response before retrying.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates maintaining long-lived jquery applications using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in maintaining long-lived jquery applications.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: The migration is repeatable, reviewed, and backed by tests.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
summary: Maintaining Long-Lived jQuery Applications is one part of the version compatibility and legacy migration workflow.
Compatibility work begins with the official upgrade guide, a dependency inventory, tests, and a controlled migration plan. Do not teach removed APIs as current jQuery 4 functionality.
Use the official API or upgrade guide for version-specific behavior and verify an example locally before relying on it.
